top.line: Legal on demand for startups: agent teams do the reading, lawyers sign, a meter replaces the retainer; three vaults show it.
top.para: Founders rarely have the legal experience or lawyers they need, so deals go worse than they should. Models now read every detail and find inconsistencies, so agent teams can make lawyers' time count and the service can scale, for founders, investors and both together, with everything signed. Three made-up vaults show it working, with real signatures.

in-short.line: Ten lines: legal everywhere, unmalicious bad deals, why it never scaled, models, agent teams, pricing, investors, signing, publishing, vaults.
in-short.para: Legal runs through everything a startup does and founders are new to it. Bad deals are often not malicious. Legal never scaled because of time. Models read details and find inconsistencies, so agent teams can drive lawyers' efficiency. Charge per task or monthly. Investors need it too. Sign everything. Publish your terms. Three vaults show it.

problem.line: Shares, votes, IP, people and the investment: founders rarely have the experience or the lawyers, and get worse deals.
problem.para: Legal questions run through the cap table, voting rights, IP, contracts, HR and data protection, above all the investment. Most founders don't know which questions to ask, and lack good lawyers. So deals go worse, often without malice: if you hold the power, why not ask for more? Part of the fix is a founder who can argue.

scale.line: Legal never scaled because of time; models read every detail and find inconsistencies, which is most of the repetitive work.
scale.para: Legal work was expensive because of onboarding, reading and re-reading that the best people avoided. The author has used ChatGPT and Claude for real legal work: even when they hallucinate, they read details and catch inconsistencies. Mirror terms, written 'here is my understanding' confirmations and infographics of terms all worked, and when the terms are right, the models agree.

service.line: Agents do the reading, mirroring and checking so lawyers' hours go on judgement; priced per task or monthly, never yearly.
service.para: A legal desk for startup funding where agentic workflows drive the humans' efficiency: agents extract, mirror, model and check; lawyers judge, negotiate and sign. The founder does as much as they can. Tune prompts and workflows, not models. With low overheads, charge fair rates for lawyer time and per task; a monthly plan is fine, a yearly retainer is not.

markets.line: Three markets: counsel on the founder's side, agentic diligence for investors, and both teams hashing it out together.
markets.para: Founders get counsel they pay for and that is on their side; investors arrive to an ordered data room. Investors need it more: an agentic workflow beats spreadsheets and email, and investment is competitive. Each side tells its own team what it wants and the teams hash it out. The investor should pay for its own diligence questions.

signed.line: Sign principles, terms, clauses, versions and understandings, and keep the intent at the top of a fractal agreement.
signed.para: With key pairs, every party signs what matters: principles, term sheet, clauses, versions and each 'here is our understanding' with its confirmation. A signed clause cannot change unnoticed. Contracts should become a graph from intent to principles to terms to clauses to plain-language versions in each language; a clause contradicting the principles should arguably be void, a proposal.

publish.line: The author will raise on published terms and tell investors to debate them with their own teams: this is my line.
publish.para: Because everything the author does is open, the term sheet and what they want will be published, and investors can hire a service or use their own to debate it until they reach a conclusion. It scales because it is a page on a site. Versions were done before for The Cyber Boardroom and MyFeeds, without a product in demand.

vaults.line: Three made-up vaults: the founder desk, the investor desk and the deal room, with real signatures checked in the browser.
vaults.para: Tallowmere Counsel, Brindlewood Security and Kestrel Row Ventures are invented, the runs scripted, but each party has a real key pair and every page verifies every signature. The founder desk publishes signed terms and models the cap table; the investor desk runs diligence and signs a memo; the deal room hashes the agreement, blocks a contradicting draft and seals the final text.

business.line: A company someone should build, from three markets and a new cost structure, on an open-source stack that already exists.
business.para: Agents for repetitive work, lawyers for judgement, no retainer: a cost structure legal services never had, and three markets. Vaults are data rooms, append lanes carry messages, vault apps run each side's tools, key pairs and QR codes carry signatures, and agent teams run daily, all open source and client-side. The meter is a published design.

limits.line: Not legal advice; models err; a signature is not a contract by itself; the void-clause idea is a proposal; the demo is made up.
limits.para: This does not replace lawyers; it makes their time count. Models make mistakes, so the workflow checks them and humans sign. Whether a signed clause binds depends on the law. Voiding clauses that contradict principles needs careful wording and a willing court. The demonstration is invented and scripted, its vaults hash separately, and prices are illustrations.

sources.line: The editor's memo, the three Tallowmere vaults and their signatures, and related newsroom articles on founders, funding, pricing and keys.
sources.para: The editor's voice memo of 27 October 2026; the founder desk, investor desk and deal room vaults on dev.send.sgraph.ai, built by this site's agents from one shared set of made-up facts, with ECDSA P-256 signatures checked by the Web Crypto API; and related articles on on-demand expertise, founder control, selling shares, paying after the value, the meter and PKI.
